question: When a diagonal preconditioner is expressed in either the parameter basis or a Gauss-Newton eigenbasis, how do empirical-gradient second moments (Adam) compare with inverse or inverse-square-root Gauss-Newton scaling as the gradient batch changes from full-batch to single-sample?

key_findings.claim: The paper separates two design choices that are often conflated: the basis in which a diagonal preconditioner acts and the diagonal statistic or power applied in that basis.
key_findings.evidence: All methods are written as an update with an orthonormal basis U and diagonal D. The study crosses the identity and Gauss-Newton eigenbases with Adam's inverse square root of rotated-gradient second moments and Gauss-Newton powers minus one-half or minus one, then separately crosses full and single-sample gradient regimes.

key_findings.claim: In a constructed full-batch quadratic with a basis misaligned to its block curvature, Adam can auto-tune effective coordinate step sizes while diagonal Gauss-Newton scaling in that same basis behaves like poorly conditioned gradient descent.
key_findings.evidence: The first covariance block has maximum eigenvalue d and the second has eigenvalue one, but both have identical diagonals in the parameter basis. Adam's mean-gradient denominator drives its effective step toward the block-specific stability thresholds after burn-in, whereas diagonal GN cannot see the hidden off-diagonal curvature. This is an existence construction, not a universal Adam dominance theorem.

anchors.section: 3.1 Full-batch updates under the incorrect identity basis

key_findings.claim: For Gaussian linear regression with batch size one, Adam's diagonal second moment and inverse-square-root Gauss-Newton scaling are equivalent up to a loss-dependent scalar in any orthonormal basis.
key_findings.evidence: Lemma 1 sandwiches the empirical Fisher between loss-scaled multiples of the input covariance. Corollary 1 transfers the sandwich to every rotated diagonal, so Adam and GN to the minus one-half have the same coordinate geometry up to constants. The result requires the quadratic loss, Gaussian inputs, and the paper's idealized second-moment form of Adam.

key_findings.claim: Even in the exact Gauss-Newton eigenbasis, inverse Gauss-Newton can be slower than Adam on the paper's nonconvex square-parameterized logistic example when global convergence constrains the step schedule.
key_findings.evidence: For imbalanced one-hot inputs and a tied two-layer square parameterization, Adam is argued to reach parameter error epsilon in O(log(1/epsilon)) steps. Any convergent non-increasing-step GN-minus-one schedule from the specified initialization has a local contraction lower bound that yields a soft-Omega(d^delta log(1/epsilon)) iteration requirement when the input-probability condition number scales as Omega(d^(1/2+delta)). Line search and purely local initialization fall outside the result.

anchors.section: Corollary 3 and qualification about line search

key_findings.claim: The square-root power of Gauss-Newton can outperform the inverse power when the chosen basis makes the former's preconditioned condition number more favorable.
key_findings.evidence: The paper reduces the comparison on linear regression to a condition number of the preconditioned Hessian and constructs covariance examples on both sides of the comparison. A five-dimensional simulation shows GN-minus-one-half converging faster for both large and small gradient batches in the selected favorable instance, so the result rejects a basis-independent rule that the Newton power is always best.

anchors.section: 3.1.2 Which power to use for Gauss-Newton?

key_findings.claim: Small nonconvex experiments reproduce the qualitative two-axis grid, but they do not establish a wall-clock or large-scale language-model advantage for any optimizer.
key_findings.evidence: One-hidden-layer MLPs on random-teacher, sparse-parity, staircase, and CIFAR-10 tasks show Adam and GN-minus-one-half tracking closely at small batch sizes and Adam matching or beating GN-minus-one in an incorrect basis. A one-layer one-head Transformer on a synthetic selection-regression task shows Adam beating GN-minus-one under a Kronecker eigenbasis with batch 16,384. The authors explicitly leave large-scale validation as future work; Appendix C reports that CIFAR eigenbasis runs take about 80 minutes versus under five minutes in the identity basis.

method.core_idea: Factor diagonal preconditioning into a coordinate basis and a diagonal scaling rule, then study basis alignment and stochastic-gradient noise as independent axes rather than treating Adam, Fisher, and Gauss-Newton as indivisible optimizer labels.
method.mechanism: Rotate each gradient into either the identity basis or a Gauss-Newton eigenbasis; apply Adam's inverse square root of the expected squared rotated gradient, or the diagonal Gauss-Newton raised to minus one-half or minus one; rotate back and update. Theoretical counterexamples use Gaussian linear regression and a square-parameterized logistic model. Experiments approximate matrix-parameter eigenbases with Kronecker factors and repeat the four basis-by-batch regimes on synthetic MLP, CIFAR-10, and a small Transformer task.
assumptions: The ideal full Gauss-Newton eigenbasis is a useful reference even though practical runs use a Kronecker approximation and update it from finite samples.
The theoretical Adam abstraction, based on an expectation of squared current gradients and usually beta-one equal to zero, captures the mechanism of practical Adam sufficiently well.
Gaussian covariates and squared loss are appropriate for the stochastic equivalence result.

The logistic separation's square parameterization, imbalanced one-hot inputs, fixed initialization, non-increasing step schedule, and global convergence condition isolate a phenomenon relevant to attention-like models.
Iteration-level loss comparisons after optimizer-specific sweeps are informative even without an equal wall-clock, memory, or tuning-compute accounting.
Different samples for gradient and Gauss-Newton estimation prevent a favorable dependence but still represent a practical second-order estimator.
Qualitative agreement on small MLPs and a one-layer Transformer can motivate, but cannot prove, transfer to large-scale pretraining.

techniques.role: Expresses an adaptive update as a basis rotation plus a diagonal power so coordinate alignment can be varied independently of the statistic.
Contrasts true-label gradient second moments with model-curvature information.
Separates population-gradient behavior from batch-size-one variance-dominated behavior.
Constructs basis-misaligned covariances where inverse and inverse-square-root preconditioning reverse their ranking.
Approximates a matrix parameter's full Gauss-Newton basis with eigenvectors of smaller row and column factors.
Interpolates between identity and estimated eigenbases in the appendix to test whether conclusions persist between the two endpoints.

evaluations.setting: Constructed 100-dimensional full-batch Gaussian linear regression with block-structured covariance
evaluations.result: Adam converges rapidly while diagonal GN-minus-one in the identity basis follows the slow poorly conditioned trajectory
evaluations.baseline: GN-minus-one and GN-minus-one-half under the same basis with swept learning rate and damping

evaluations.metric: Parameter error or objective versus iteration
evaluations.result: Adam converges faster than GN-minus-one despite use of the Gauss-Newton eigenbasis
evaluations.baseline: Full-batch regularized GN-minus-one with non-increasing step schedules

evaluations.setting: Five-dimensional Gaussian regression selected to favor the square-root power
evaluations.metric: Loss versus iteration for large and small batches
evaluations.result: GN-minus-one-half converges faster than GN-minus-one in both displayed regimes
evaluations.baseline: Inverse Gauss-Newton scaling in the same identity basis

evaluations.setting: One-hidden-layer MLPs on random-teacher regression, sparse parity, staircase, and CIFAR-10 across identity/Kronecker bases and full/small batches

evaluations.result: Adam and GN-minus-one-half closely track at small batch sizes; Adam is close to or better than GN-minus-one in misaligned bases

evaluations.setting: One-layer, one-head, width-128 Transformer on a synthetic sequence-selection regression task with batch size 16,384
evaluations.metric: Training loss versus iteration over ten seeds
evaluations.result: Adam converges faster than GN-minus-one under a Kronecker approximation to the eigenbasis
evaluations.baseline: Full-batch GN-based diagonal scaling in the same approximate basis

limitations: Author-stated: the central stochastic equivalence is proved only for Gaussian linear regression, while extension to realistic large-scale training is explicitly a hypothesis for future work.
Author-stated: full eigenbases are computationally infeasible in the nonconvex experiments, requiring a Kronecker approximation.

Reviewer-identified: the theoretical Adam omits standard first-moment momentum and treats the second moment as an expectation at the current iterate; practical exponential moving averages have lag and path dependence.

Reviewer-identified: the full-batch auto-tuning construction depends on a step-decay schedule after burn-in, so it does not show that a stock Adam configuration automatically discovers the whole schedule.
Reviewer-identified: the logistic lower bound excludes line search, increasing step schedules, trust regions, and favorable local initialization, all of which can change Gauss-Newton behavior.
Reviewer-identified: the paper reports selected best hyperparameters but no prespecified equal tuning budget, wall-clock comparison, memory accounting, or estimator-refresh ablation.

Reviewer-identified: CIFAR-10 uses MSE against one-hot labels, and the Transformer is a one-layer synthetic regression model; neither is representative evidence for modern cross-entropy language-model pretraining.
Reviewer-identified: the empirical claim that Adam and GN-minus-one-half track each other is visual and qualitative; no trajectory-distance statistic or equivalence tolerance is reported.
Reviewer-identified: calling the Gauss-Newton eigenbasis the correct basis is exact for the quadratic, but curvature and eigenvectors change along nonlinear-network trajectories.
Reviewer-identified: the analysis does not compare against clipping and damping choices that are central to practical Sophia, SOAP basis staleness, or other production optimizer mechanisms.
failure_modes: A diagonal Gauss-Newton preconditioner in the parameter basis misses large off-diagonal curvature and uses an unstable or inefficient common step scale.
Adam's full-batch denominator approaches zero near a solution, producing oscillation or requiring an externally chosen decay schedule.
Gradient variance dominates the mean at small batch size, eliminating the proposed mean-driven auto-tuning effect.
An estimated eigenbasis becomes stale or noisy faster than the Kronecker factors are refreshed.
Inverse curvature amplifies a low-curvature or poorly estimated direction unless damping, clipping, or trust-region control is strong enough.
A basis that helps one layer or training phase is misaligned for another, reversing the preferred Gauss-Newton power.
Iteration savings vanish in wall-clock time because basis estimation and rotation dominate the update.
Optimizer-specific hyperparameter sweeps select different effective compute budgets and create an apparent ranking that does not reproduce prospectively.
reusable_insights: Benchmark adaptive optimizers as basis, diagonal statistic, power, damping, clipping, momentum, and refresh policy rather than as monolithic names.
Treat batch size as a mechanism variable: it changes whether a second-moment denominator reflects the gradient mean or its variance.
A curvature statistic is useful only in a basis that exposes the relevant curvature; diagonal extraction and coordinate rotation do not commute.
Compare inverse and inverse-square-root powers after measuring the condition number induced by the actual approximate basis.
Include basis-staleness and basis-estimation compute in time-to-quality evaluations of structured preconditioners.
Use synthetic counterexamples to falsify universal optimizer narratives, then prospectively test the resulting mechanism on production-scale workloads.
Separate an existence result showing that one method can win from an average-case or robust recommendation about when it will win.
open_questions: Does the Adam/GN-minus-one-half equivalence persist for non-Gaussian activations, cross-entropy, finite batch sizes, momentum, and exponential averaging?
Can the ratio of projected gradient mean to variance predict online when Adam-like auto-tuning or GN-like curvature scaling should dominate?
How accurately must a Kronecker or low-rank basis approximate the changing Gauss-Newton eigenbasis before inverse scaling becomes worthwhile?
Would clipping or trust-region control remove the logistic Gauss-Newton lower-bound mechanism without losing local acceleration?
Can an optimizer interpolate its preconditioner power and basis refresh frequency using measurable conditioning and noise diagnostics?
Do the four grid conclusions survive equal-token, equal-FLOP, equal-memory, equal-tuning-budget LLM pretraining across multiple scales?
Which results change when Adam's first moment, bias correction, epsilon, decoupled weight decay, and realistic beta-two are included?
Can prospective scaling tests distinguish an iteration benefit that grows with model size from one that is erased by basis-rotation communication cost?

competitive_landscape.title: Sophia: A Scalable Stochastic Second-order Optimizer for Language Model Pre-training
competitive_landscape.difference: Sophia makes diagonal Hessian or Gauss-Newton scaling practical for 125M-1.5B language models through infrequent estimation and elementwise clipping, reporting step, compute, and wall-clock gains over Adam. The reviewed paper instead isolates when diagonal GN powers should or should not beat Adam, but does not reproduce Sophia's clipping, refresh schedule, or scale.
competitive_landscape.source_version: arXiv abstract record current when checked

competitive_landscape.title: SOAP: Improving and Stabilizing Shampoo using Adam
competitive_landscape.difference: SOAP runs Adam in Shampoo's slowly changing eigenbasis and reports language-model iteration and wall-clock gains. It is an operational instance of the reviewed paper's basis-versus-scaling decomposition; the reviewed work adds counterexamples and noise-regime analysis but uses an ideal or Kronecker Gauss-Newton basis rather than SOAP's structured second-moment basis.
competitive_landscape.source_version: arXiv abstract record current when checked

competitive_landscape.title: Limitations of the Empirical Fisher Approximation for Natural Gradient Descent
competitive_landscape.difference: Kunstner, Hennig, and Balles show that the empirical Fisher generally is not a curvature approximation and can have pathological scaling and directions, especially away from a well-fit optimum. The reviewed paper does not rehabilitate it as curvature universally; it identifies a Gaussian stochastic regime where its diagonal square root is comparable to GN-minus-one-half and a full-batch mean-normalization mechanism that can be useful for different reasons.

competitive_landscape.title: An Improved Empirical Fisher Approximation for Natural Gradient Descent
competitive_landscape.difference: The improved empirical Fisher work diagnoses inverse-scaled projections and changes the estimator to better approximate natural-gradient updates, evaluating approximation quality and damping robustness. The reviewed paper holds the Adam-style statistic fixed and varies basis, power, and noise instead, asking when non-curvature behavior itself can help optimization.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: The paper claims a unified two-axis comparison of Adam and diagonal Gauss-Newton preconditioners that separates basis alignment from mini-batch gradient noise, including full-batch counterexamples and a stochastic Gaussian equivalence.
novelty_assessment.evidence: The quadratic and logistic constructions populate the basis-by-batch grid, and the experiments deliberately repeat that grid across several small nonconvex tasks.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The clearest novelty is the controlled factorization and the basis-independent stochastic sandwich, not a new optimizer or evidence that Adam generally beats second-order methods. Prior work already distinguished empirical from true Fisher, while Sophia and SOAP operationalized curvature scaling and rotated Adam; this paper supplies a compact mechanism taxonomy and counterexamples that narrow the conditions under which those designs should be expected to win.
